lesson_title: The Compass That Flinched: Electromagnetism and Faraday's Law
hook_text: Physicists spent eleven years waiting for magnets to make electricity. Nothing happened. One missing word changed the world.
clip_script: Copenhagen, 1820. A lecturer named Oersted switches on a current — and a compass at the edge of his bench FLINCHES. Off: it settles. On: it flinches again. A wire was shoving a magnet without touching it, and suddenly electricity and magnetism were one subject. So everyone asked the reverse: can a magnet make electricity? Across Europe, powerful magnets were laid beside coils of wire, meters watched, breath held. Zero. For ELEVEN YEARS, zero. Everyone was missing a single word: CHANGE. Faraday found it. Move the magnet toward the coil — current. Freeze — dead, instantly, even with the magnet resting inside. Pull back — current again, reversed. A parked magnet makes nothing; a MOVING one generates every time, and the faster it moves, the more you harvest. Wind more turns and every loop catches the change — a hundred and fifty loops push a hundred and fifty times harder. One catch: the current is contrary. Shove a north pole in and the coil turns its own north face at you and shoves back. You pay in effort; the wires pay you back in energy. Scale it up — spinning coils, roaring turbines — and that is every power station feeding the grid. Your phone charges tonight on one word that took eleven years to find.
visual_style: A candle-lit 1820 lecture bench with a twitching compass; a montage of stalled experiments and flat meter needles as the years tick by; a magnet plunging into a coil with the needle leaping; finale of turbines spinning into a glowing national grid.
mood: Historical detective story — a decade-long dead end cracked by a single word.
pacing: Period-drama open, tense stalled middle, accelerating triumphant close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and own the law that lights the country.
